To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

reading emotion laden literature is a complex process, which involves emotion-related structures in the amygdala and emotion-related structures in lateral prefrontal cortex, anterior temporal cortex, and temporo-parietal cortex.
the processing of emotion in a second language is less differentiated and less emotionally arousing than in the native language.

reading emotion laden literary texts in L1 is associated with stronger and more differentiated neural activity in emotion related structures than reading such texts in L2, which may be due to the fact that the L1 is acquired at a much earlier age and is therefore more deeply embedded into the brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how late bilinguals process emotional content in their native versus second language.
the question how late bilinguals process emotion laden texts in their first and second languages and how this relates to emotional experience and neural activity.
the question of whether the reading experience is the same for L1 and L2.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
reading emotion laden literature is a complex process that involves a network of brain regions that are sensitive to language proficiency.
reading emotion laden text is a complex cognitive and emotional process, which involves the interaction of different neural systems.

L1 reading of literature elicits stronger emotional responses than L2 reading of literature, but this does not necessarily imply that L2 reading of emotion laden literature is not effective in evoking emotional responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the processing of emotion-laden literature is a highly complex process, and it involves a network of brain regions, including those associated with emotional processing, language processing, Theory of Mind and discourse comprehension.
L1 reading of emotional texts is more emotionally engaging than L2 reading of the same texts.
L2 reading is not as emotionally engaging as L1 reading.
The main takeaway from our work is that
even in late bilinguals, the emotional experience of reading is not the same in L1 as it is in L2.
L2 proficiency is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a full emotional engagement with literary texts.
the processing of emotional stimuli is not necessarily the same across different languages, even in proficient second language speakers.
